situations.TextKey: A cabinet of blackened oak sorts papers by guilt, not alphabet. One drawer opens with a sound like a verdict being reconsidered.

value.Purpose: choose a card for the cabinet to refile
choose the card that will be Misfiled
choose a card to pull out of the file

situations.TextKey: The application comes back under a title nobody chose, fifty Gold falls out of a fold in the paper, and a second document quietly leaves the alphabet.
One obsolete procedure tears loose. Two of the cabinet's own forms come away with it.
A brass drawer offers certified copies of anything placed inside. The copies are perfect. The drawer is hungry.

value.Purpose: choose a card to have certified in duplicate
choose the card the drawer seals

situations.TextKey: The drawer returns two of what you gave it, and one duplicate notice for its trouble.
The stamp is yours. The drawer keeps one of your papers sealed until it is satisfied it is not a copy.
A slate fee table updates while you read it. Each new line looks older and more legally binding than the last.

value.Purpose: improve a card

situations.TextKey: The table accepts the ruinous sum and stamps two procedures as properly improved.
Seventy-five Gold is refunded on the spot. The refund is provisional, and the audit is already scheduled.
Behind a dusty desk lie lost seals, receipt spikes, wax knives, and forms nobody wants to admit they misplaced.

value.Purpose: choose a card to leave for identification

situations.TextKey: The desk takes it away for examination. Whatever comes back will have been improved by the attention.
The tag is yours, and so is the unsigned form somebody left inside the parcel.
A vendor unfolds a counter covered in seals, receipts, and legally glowing merchandise. Every item has been licensed by someone who is currently denying responsibility.
The prices are official, which somehow makes them worse.

value.Purpose: choose a card to have struck from your file

Choices.TextKey: Have a card struck from your file — 75 Gold
Thank the vendor and move on.

situations.TextKey: The vendor hands over something wrapped in a receipt. The receipt continues on the back, where it explains who is collecting your next fee.
A heavy ledger invites formal complaints. Its previous entries are complaining about the complaints below them.

value.Purpose: choose a card to complain about

situations.TextKey: One useless procedure is struck from your file, and the next office is instructed to let the first filing against you go.
Your signature buys you a procedure of your own — and a witness who will be watching how you file it.
At the end of a bench sits a counter that trades lost waiting time for small official advantages.

value.Purpose: improve a card

situations.TextKey: The ticket is yours. The counter, in return, opens late tomorrow.
A procedure improves while you wait. A notice of delay takes your former place.
A clerk looks up, understands almost everything, and reaches for a stamp. This is either a miracle or a trap.

value.Purpose: choose the card to have stamped

situations.TextKey: The stamp lands slightly off-centre, which is apparently what makes it free. The clerk files a form that was never signed.
You arrive by the short corridor. Whoever was waiting for you had to run, and nobody is paying for the paperwork.
Three witnesses swear you were here before. Unfortunately, none of them agree on what you were doing.

value.Purpose: choose the statement to withdraw

situations.TextKey: The witness produces something official from an inside pocket, and two duplicate notices from the other one.
One false statement leaves your file. A summons arrives to replace it.
The contradictions are useful. So is the protection they buy you — and so, unfortunately, is the witness now attached to your filing.
A sealed side door claims to lead directly to the right corridor. The seal disagrees in very small print.
The corridor is exactly as advertised, and so is the summons that was pinned to the other side of the door.
The ward is yours. Word travels: whatever is waiting has been told to take you seriously.
For one impossible minute, no one is responsible for anything. A cup of tea steams beside an abandoned ledger.

value.Purpose: improve a card

situations.TextKey: It tastes like dust, mercy, and exactly a fifth of your maximum health.
One genuinely useful correction, and one clerk's private arrangement about hours worked after the counter closes.
A filing cabinet opens helpfully. The other furniture watches it with professional suspicion.

value.Purpose: choose a card to file away for good
choose a card to be replaced with a better form

Choices.TextKey: Let it find a better form.

situations.TextKey: One unnecessary item is filed somewhere you will never have to visit.
The cabinet knows a form that does what you meant. It puts the new one where you will find it first.
An old receipt proves that you once nearly did everything correctly. The ink is faded, but the implication is useful.
A clerk grudgingly pays out an administrative refund of seventy-five Gold.
The claim is accepted, at a rate that depends entirely on how quickly you finish the next piece of work.
A wall map shows three routes to the same office. Two exist only on Tuesdays, and one is arguing with itself.
You arrive early and unannounced. Nobody has authorised payment for work done off the route.
The annotations are useful and terrifying in equal measure. One of them turns out to be the wrong form entirely.
The creases cross out a corridor that was never there. You keep the map. The map keeps handing you the wrong form.
A narrow window opens into an archive older than the city ordinance. A hand made of dust offers two kinds of help.

value.Purpose: choose a method to submit for preservation

situations.TextKey: The folder still remembers how to be useful. The terms under which it was lent are printed very small.
The archive takes the method away to copy it properly. What comes back is better, and it is stamped as the original.
A prophecy about you has been filed under a classification that does not exist. It is accurate, which is the part nobody can explain, and it is in the wrong drawer, which is the part everyone can.

value.Purpose: choose a card to be refiled as something else
choose the card the archive will misfile
choose the card the revision is authorized for

situations.TextKey: The prophecy is refiled as something else entirely. In exchange the archive takes one of your own procedures and files it just as badly.
The wrong code becomes the right one. One of your procedures is authorized to revise itself, and an unfinished citation is filed behind you.
An index corrects itself while you watch. Two of its corrections are improvements. One of them is a black rectangle where a word used to be.

value.Purpose: choose two cards for the index to correct
choose which correction the index redacted
choose the entry to strike from the index
choose up to two cards the index will misfile

situations.TextKey: Two procedures come back better. One of them comes back with half of itself missing.
One entry leaves your file for good. The index, offended, misfiles two others out of spite.
A reading room stands locked behind glass. Inside, a single volume is open at a page you can almost read. A supervisor's chair faces it, empty, and recently warm.

value.Purpose: choose the card to be illuminated

Choices.TextKey: Copy a single illuminated passage. (40 Gold)

situations.TextKey: You are allowed the rare volume. Somebody stands behind you the whole time, and every fourth thing you write down is taken away and blacked out.
The gold buys an hour and a good pen. The initial you copy is worth more than the passage it opens.
Nothing is read. The quiet does what quiet does, and a fifth of what the archives have taken from you comes back.
Someone has been borrowing from this archive for longer than the archive has existed. They are unfailingly polite, they return everything, and everything they return is better than it was.

value.Purpose: choose a volume to lend the borrower

Choices.TextKey: Lend one of your own volumes.

value.Purpose: choose a card the borrower corrects

situations.TextKey: The borrower takes it with both hands. You will not have it for the next piece of work — but if that work goes well, what comes back is better than what went out.
The notes are somebody else's, and good. The claim slip that comes stapled to them is yours now.
The account is closed, courteously. You are given tea, an hour's rest, and one correction you did not ask for.
It is warm. It is also, in some sense nobody wants to define, still in use — and the part of you that is now lending it out is not getting it back.
A shelf that gives exactly as much as it is given, and classifies exactly as well as it is argued with. A loose label hangs from one end, printed on both sides.

value.Purpose: choose an entry to submit to the shelf
choose the card the shelf reclassifies

situations.TextKey: The shelf takes what you no longer want, returns something you might, and pays fifty Gold for the inconvenience.
You win the argument. The shelf reclassifies a different card of yours out of pure spite, and blacks out half of it on the way.
Reversible, as promised. So is the shelf's memory of where your things belong — for the next two pieces of work, something of yours starts in the wrong place.
Two hands have been arguing in the margins of this volume for four hundred years. Both are right. Neither has noticed the other is dead.

value.Purpose: choose two cards to bind into a pair
choose the card to carry the reply
choose a card the practice improves

situations.TextKey: You copy the pair of them onto two of your own procedures. From now on, playing either fetches the other.
You settle the argument in gold leaf. Whichever of your procedures carries the reply opens every fight worth a card and a little cover.
The vellum comes up beautifully. One of your own procedures is improved by the practice, and a leaf of the scraped ink follows you into the next room.
A volume has been reserved for a reader who never came. The reservation is still valid. The register beside it has a blank line, and a pen.

Choices.TextKey: Enter another name in the register.

situations.TextKey: The volume is yours, and it stays reserved a while longer — it is not on the table for the opening of the next piece of work, and when it arrives it arrives free.
You sit in the reader's chair for as long as nobody comes. Nobody comes.
Seventy Gold for a signature that is not yours. One of your own cards is now registered to somebody else, and cannot be filed until something else has been.
A brass slot in the wall, worn smooth. Everything the archives have ever lost went in here, and the archives have never once admitted that anything comes back out.

value.Purpose: choose a bad idea to return
choose a card to reach back for

situations.TextKey: It goes in without a sound. Forty Gold comes back, which is more than the idea was worth, and the slot remembers it — the archives never truly lose anything.
Your arm goes in further than the wall is thick. What comes out is something you gave up on, exactly as you gave it up — along with somebody else's claim slip.
A portrait of an archivist whose face has been officially removed. The frame, the hands and the signature are immaculate. Somebody went to the trouble of blacking out only the face.

value.Purpose: choose the card that learns its own name

situations.TextKey: The restorer takes the money and returns a cameo with nothing on it. It is the face. It is also, from now on, whichever of your cards the archive would rather not see.
You do not learn the name. You learn that it HAS one — and you write that on one of your own cards, which will not be written over so easily again.
Some faces were removed for a reason. Walking away is worth a little of what the archives have cost you.
A stoppered bottle labelled with a date, a place, and one hour that nobody accounted for. It is warm and it is faintly ticking.

value.Purpose: choose the card to bind the hour into

Choices.TextKey: Bind the hour into a card.

situations.TextKey: Two rounds of somebody else's afternoon. It is glorious. The third round is when the hour is noticed missing, and the archives take it back out of yours.
The hour goes into the paper. Whatever you write on it is never discarded, and the second turn you are still holding it, it is worth more.
A window onto the department that files the dead. Two ledgers lie open: one of lives that stopped mid-sentence, one of accounts nobody ever closed.

value.Purpose: choose the entry to close
choose the entry to finish properly

situations.TextKey: It fits badly and it heals a great deal. The clerk notes the loan; somewhere ahead of you, something now has an hour of it too — and the department pays well for the paperwork.
It costs eight of your own to close somebody else's. One entry leaves your file entirely; another is finished properly, at last.
The clerk from the city offices is here, three floors below where anyone can find them, and very pleased to see you. They have been reassigned. Nobody has told them what to.

value.Purpose: choose the card to be amended

Choices.TextKey: Ask how the Clerk has been.

situations.TextKey: They tell you the correct wording with their hand over their mouth. Half of it is blacked out before you get it down — file it anyway and the correction sticks for good.
It is laminated, it is expired, and it works. Thirty-five Gold falls out of the sleeve, which the clerk pretends not to notice.
Badly, thank you for asking. Nobody has, in some time. It costs them nothing to say so and it does you a surprising amount of good.
One table in the whole archive where nothing is happening. A vow is carved into it, a forbidden volume is chained to it, and the chair is still warm from whoever chose neither.

Choices.TextKey: Take the Vow of Silent Scholarship.

situations.TextKey: Three filings a turn, no more, until the next piece of work is done. Nothing enforces it. That is rather the point.
It is worth it. It is also watched — you carry a leaf of its ink into the next room, and every fourth thing you file there is read over your shoulder.
You sit at the quiet table and read nothing at all. It is the first quarter-hour of the run that belongs to you.
A wax seal pressed into the wall itself, facing inward. Whatever it was sealing, it was sealing it away from the archive, not from you.

value.Purpose: choose two cards the breaking seal catches
choose two cards the seal improves
choose which of them the seal blacked out
choose which of them the seal misfiled

Choices.TextKey: Press the seal into your skin.

situations.TextKey: The wax comes away in one piece and inverts in your hand. Two of your cards are misfiled and blacked out in the confusion; the sealstone is worth both of them.
You press it back the way it was facing. Two procedures are improved by the discipline; one comes out half-erased and the other in the wrong drawer.
It does not hurt and it does not come off. You are, from now on, marginally more of a document — and the archives have already started filing you.
The aisle ends in a desk that was not there a moment ago, and a librarian who has been waiting at it for a very long time. They know what you have thrown away. They are not judging. They have a list.

value.Purpose: choose the book the Librarian has been keeping
choose the volume to be forgotten

Choices.TextKey: Ask the Librarian to forget a volume.

situations.TextKey: They do not have to look it up. What comes back is what you gave up on, one improvement further along, and it knows its own name now.
They take it off the list, which is a different and much quieter thing than destroying it. Whatever it was costing you stops.
They point down an aisle that was not there either. Whatever is at the end of it arrived in a hurry and diminished, nobody is paying you for the shortcut, and there is a procedure waiting.
The water runs over pale stones and takes nothing with it that does not want to go. Somebody has set a cup on the bank, upside down, for whoever comes next.

value.Purpose: choose what to wash away
choose what to wash carefully

situations.TextKey: One thing goes downstream, and you feel a little better for having let it.
The rowan leans over the water. What you washed comes out blessed, and so do you.
It keeps. The first demand you settle in full on the next ordinary road will grant one more leave to pass than it would have.
The hedge is grown through with notices — some nailed, some written straight onto the bark. Every one of them says the same thing in a different hand: not this way.

value.Purpose: choose what to leave in the gap
choose what the hedge will knot

Choices.TextKey: Ask the hedge to mark the path.

situations.TextKey: Thirty-five Gold buys the paperwork, and the hedge opens exactly wide enough for one thing to be left behind.
Ninety Gold's worth of shortcut, and a hedge's demand waiting at the next ordinary fight. Nobody will hold it against you afterwards; they will only take it out of you.
A knot is tied where the way changes. One of your procedures carries it now.
She is sitting on the milestone rather than beside it, which is either rude or a legal position. She does not ask where you are going. She asks what you would give to get there sooner.

value.Purpose: choose what she will knot
choose what she will improve
choose the memory to give her

situations.TextKey: She ties it into one of your procedures and improves the knot while she is at it.
She takes it out of your file and out of you, and pays for it in old coin.
It is shorter. Whatever is waiting on it is diminished by the hurry, nobody is paying you for the shortcut, and there is something at the end worth having.
Two hedges, one path, and four opinions about which of them is older. Everybody present is holding a document, and none of the documents agree.

value.Purpose: choose what to concede
choose two to improve in the mediation

situations.TextKey: You are covered — twice over — and everyone on the road afterwards has standing to object. There is a purse in it if you get through them.
You give way, and it costs a little of you and one of your own procedures.
Two procedures come out of it better. Your own leave to pass went into the settlement.
The circle is perfect and nobody made it. Standing outside it you can hear a discussion; standing inside it you would be part of one.

value.Purpose: choose what to offer the circle

situations.TextKey: It costs you something to be a member. You come out wearing a cap that puts every third thing you do to a vote.
One procedure goes into the ring. Two others come back improved, and nobody says by whom.
You will be counted at the end of every turn of the next ordinary fight: one real card, or three. Get through it without failing the count and the ring will give you a voice.
The web is between two thorn branches and it is written on. Not marked — written, in a hand that runs clockwise and gets smaller towards the middle.

value.Purpose: choose what the exception covers
choose what the cut costs you

situations.TextKey: It costs you something to read that far in. One of your procedures acquires an older right than the one that burns it.
One procedure goes with it, and something on the next road will remember that you cut.
A hundred Gold for a signature nobody read. Somebody on the next road will have standing because of it.
The line crosses the road and has been crossing it, by the look of the grass, for longer than the road has been here. Nothing in it hurries. Nothing in it stops.

value.Purpose: choose two to put in order while you wait

situations.TextKey: It takes most of the afternoon. Two procedures are properly filed by the end of it, and you are rested.
Something bites. There is a rare thing lying where the line was, and coin beside it.
You are in the procession now, and it has an order: nothing cheaper after something dear, within a turn. Win an ordinary fight without stepping out of it and they will mark you.
There is no bridge. There is a toll, and a keeper, and a very old argument about whether the absence of a bridge is a reason not to charge for crossing it.
What is laid out is laid out; there will be no more of it.

value.Purpose: choose what to have struck from your file

Choices.TextKey: Have something struck from your file — 63 Gold

situations.TextKey: Eighty-five Gold's worth of being right, and a crossing's demand waiting at the next ordinary fight.
Twice covered, unpaid, and something worth having at the end of the next ordinary fight.
The rain arrives the way rain does on this road: all at once, and with the air of having been waiting. The rowan is the only thing for a mile that is not getting wet underneath.

value.Purpose: choose what the rowan shelters

situations.TextKey: It takes an hour and it is worth an hour.
It says yes the way trees do. One of your procedures is under the branches now, permanently.
You are wet and shorter of breath, and for the next two ordinary fights you start with more in hand than you would have.
Most of it is under the turf. What is above says a distance and half a name, and the distance is wrong for anywhere that still exists.

value.Purpose: choose what the stones will witness
choose the mark to bury

Choices.TextKey: Bury one of your own marks beside it.

situations.TextKey: The stones watched, which is a thing they can be made to do again. One of your procedures carries their attention now.
It goes somewhere smaller than it should. Nobody pays you for the detour, and there is something rare at the end of it.
It goes under the turf with the rest. It costs you a little of yourself, and a hundred Gold comes up where it went down.
The cart smells of tallow and beeswax and something underneath that is neither. He sells light, and light on this road is a legal commodity.

value.Purpose: choose what to trade for wax

situations.TextKey: What is laid out is laid out; there will be no more of it.
Fifty Gold for a light that lasts one fight, and lights it well: you begin with more to spend and leave to spend it.
One procedure goes onto the cart. Thirty-five Gold comes off it.
Three of them are low and bright and have been argued over. The road star, the root star, and the one over the hill that nobody around here will name out loud.

value.Purpose: choose two the root star improves

situations.TextKey: It costs a little of you to look that long. The next two ordinary fights open with leave to pass.
Two procedures come out of it better, and one of them is kept warm afterwards.
There is something rare in it, and something under the hill now knows your face.
Nothing here has a right to anything. The grass is long, the light is level, and for the length of a field there is nobody to be answerable to.

value.Purpose: choose two to practise
choose what to leave in the meadow

situations.TextKey: Two procedures are better for the hour, and nobody has to be told.
It stays in the grass. You go on lighter.
Nothing happens for a long time, which is the whole of what the meadow has to offer, and it is a great deal.
A leaf the size of a hand, pressed flat and written on both sides. It is addressed to you, it is dated tomorrow, and it is signed with a paw print and a seal.

value.Purpose: choose two to put in order

situations.TextKey: Two procedures are put in order for it, and the next hard room finds you already covered.
It is filed. Everybody on the next ordinary road is answering paperwork instead of you, and the largest of them has standing to be annoyed about it.
It costs you something to carry a complaint about yourself. The first party to lay a hand on you will be answering it.
They are going the other way, unhurried, carrying nothing you can name. Every one of them looks at you as they pass, and every one of them is kind about it.

value.Purpose: choose what to give them
choose what comes back improved

Choices.TextKey: Give the procession something of yours.
Follow them farther than three steps.

situations.TextKey: It takes a moment and it is the right moment. You are the better for it in a way that lasts.
Three steps is guest-right. It costs you seven of yourself, and the road looks after its guests from here on.
They take it without breaking step. A hundred Gold is in your hand and another of your procedures is better than it was.
You come back whole and twelve short, wearing their brooch and carrying something rare. Everything on the next road has heard where you have been.
A stair cut down into a shaft that has not held water in living memory. The marks are still there, and so is the official who reads them, and he is reading them.
He writes down the lowest mark, which is the true one, and it costs you six of yourself to be measured honestly. He gives you the cup he measures with.
Ninety Gold for a level that suits everybody. It is entered in the register, and the register follows you for two rooms.
Nothing is written down at all, which is restful. The next office you meet has to start from the beginning, and starts with you.
Sealed since a year nobody can name, and full — you can hear it. The seal is a clay disc the size of a hand, and it is the only thing between the grain and everyone who is hungry.

value.Purpose: choose two to put in order

situations.TextKey: A hundred and thirty Gold's worth of grain and something that was buried with it. You carry it out yourself, and you carry it for two rooms.
What is allotted is allotted. It is a great deal of food and slightly less of you afterwards.
You put the tally back in order. Two of your procedures come out of it better, and the granary enters your name for having done it.
Red linen, carried the length of the corridor by people who do not look at it. There is no body in it. There is a very great deal of paperwork in it.

value.Purpose: choose what goes into the wrapping
choose two to correct from the wrapping

situations.TextKey: You walk with them as far as the turn, and one of your own procedures goes into the wrapping. The linen keeps what it is given.
It parts, and what is inside is a filing you can improve twice. The corridor closes behind you for having done it.
It is much farther than it looked and it costs twelve of you to arrive. At the gate they cut you a knot of the linen, which is not a small thing to be given.
An oval cut deep into the wall with nothing inside it. Whoever it belonged to has been removed from the record so thoroughly that the hole itself is now the record.

value.Purpose: choose two to sign
choose what is scraped out with it

situations.TextKey: It fits. Two of your procedures are the better for having a name over them, and every office for the next three rooms has a name to enter.
You take the hole down to clean stone. Something of yours goes with it and so does seven of you.
A chip of the empty oval, pocket-sized. It is a cartouche with nobody in it, which turns out to be a useful thing to be carrying in a building like this.
The tablet describes, in the past tense, everything you are about to do in this corridor. Three scribes stand around it. One of them is already writing the next line.

value.Purpose: choose the line to correct
choose the first to be struck out
choose the second to be struck out

situations.TextKey: One line, and the thing it described is a different thing now — a better one — and there is fifty Gold in the correction fee for having found the error yourself.

They will not give it up here. They will be waiting on the next ordinary stretch of corridor, all three of them, writing about whoever is standing there — and there is a relic in it if you take the tablet off them.
Signing makes it true, and two of your own procedures are struck out to make room for it. The paperwork that follows follows you for two rooms.
Three of them, a small fire, and a great deal that is not theirs laid out on a cloth. They are not hiding. Nobody licensed comes down this far.
Seventy Gold, and they hand over something they clearly want rid of. The next corridor knows where you got it.

You are in on it now, which means you are in on it when they are found. It will be the next ordinary stretch of corridor, the lamp will go out first, and the take is a hundred and twenty Gold and a piece of what was in there.
A hundred Gold off the cloth while they are arguing. They come looking, and they are still looking two rooms later.
One donkey, three tokens, three offices — each of which counted it, and each of which is correct. The donkey is standing in the corridor waiting to be resolved.

value.Purpose: choose what is broken with them

situations.TextKey: The oldest count wins, which is the tidiest answer and pays seventy-five Gold. You carry the other two tokens out with you.
There is no donkey now, officially. It costs you a little blood and one of your own procedures, and you come out of it more solid than you went in.
It knows a way through. Where it stops there is water and something somebody left behind.
Four jars on a shelf, each labelled with what it holds and each label in a different hand. Only one of them is what it says. You may open one.

value.Purpose: choose three to enter under the name

situations.TextKey: It is empty, and the emptiness is the point: it is a jar for holding a breath somebody else has finished with.
Twelve more of you, all at once, and a great deal of it in your mouth for the next room.
A hundred and fifty Gold in old coin, and every bit of it wants carrying.
The name in it is not yours, but three of your procedures are entered under it, and the next office finds you very thoroughly on the register.
Every weight in the room is stamped with the royal cartouche and no two of them agree. The scale in the middle is the only honest object here, and it is waiting.
You take the heaviest, which makes you heavier, and every measure for the next two rooms is taken against it.
The lightest weighs almost nothing, and so, briefly, do you. You come out whole and eight short of what you were.
Fifteen of you and one royal weight, broken in half on the floor. Half a royal weight still weighs whatever it is told to weigh, which is the whole of the trick.
The scale is set up properly, the offerings are stacked beside it, and the thing waiting under the scale for whatever fails the weighing has been waiting a very long time.
Sixty Gold onto the pan. It is accepted, which is not the same as being weighed, and you are the better for the arrangement.
You are weighed, and what you are found to be worth is handed to you. The finding is entered, and the corridor has the entry before you do.
A hundred and twenty Gold that was meant for somebody who is not coming. It is noted. It is noted for three rooms.
Every hand's breadth of it is a grievance somebody scratched in and nobody answered, going back so far that the oldest are underneath the newest and the wall is thicker for it.

value.Purpose: choose two complaints worth making properly
choose the complaint to withdraw

situations.TextKey: You scratch in your two corrections, which is two of your procedures improved and one more complaint on a wall of them. The next office has read it.
You take one grievance off the wall — yours — and it costs six of you to have never had it.
All of them, in order, which takes as long as it takes. What you carry away is the chisel somebody left in the wall, and two rooms' worth of doubt about everything.
A table across the corridor, a copper bowl on the table, and a bearer beside the bowl who has been told what the tithe is and has no authority to hear anything else.

value.Purpose: choose two the receipt covers
upgrade a card
remove a card from your deck

situations.TextKey: A part of what you carry into the bowl, and the receipt is worth having: two of your procedures come back stamped.
More than a third, which nobody asks twice about. What comes back out of the bowl was not put there by you.
You keep what you carry, which is the whole of the point. The bearer writes nothing down and sends word ahead, and the word is waiting on the next ordinary road.
A throne with the name cut out of it — not worn away, cut, carefully, by somebody who was paid to and knew exactly how much had to go. The gold leaf around the hole is untouched.

value.Purpose: choose the two that go with the name

situations.TextKey: You cut a name back into it, which is eight of yourself and a very great deal of nerve. The tablet they used for the erasure is still under the seat, and it works both ways.
The rest of it goes, and two of your own procedures go with it because the chisel does not distinguish. The corridor afterwards is not a restful place.
A hundred and fifty Gold's worth of leaf off a throne nobody sits on, and three rooms of paperwork about where it went.
The festival is held on a fixed day, which was fixed by a calendar that has since been corrected twice. It is being held anyway, today, by people who are not going to be told otherwise.

value.Purpose: choose the deed the standard honours
choose the deed the standard honours
choose the working the standard honours
choose the working the standard honours

Correctness is not a discount: the first measure you MEET each round is filed, and filing costs you 1 Paperwork.
This animal has been entered in the register this many times. At 3 the entries are settled: the load goes on you, and the tally starts again.
Every measure that resolves, right or wrong, enters this animal once more. The third entry is the one you carry: 2 Burdened, or 1 if that third measure was met.
Everything was presented and everything was correct: this envoy has nothing left to hold up, and takes 50% more damage until its next turn.
This envoy reads what was left in your hand. End a turn empty-handed and a measure resolves: if you met it, the envoy is exposed until its next turn; if you missed it, you are Inscribed.
The gang has lost its step. Its next Rope Snap carries 6 more damage, and the strain is spent doing it.
This gang pulls in step. Whenever Fatigue actually takes Energy out of your hands, it strains — and its next Rope Snap carries the strain.
How far this conscript has got. At 2 it leaves the fight — and the room counts as resolved.
This conscript is not fighting you, it is leaving. Break the rest of the gang's Block during your turn and it gets 1 Escape closer; at 2 it is gone.
Hauled out of what the bureaucracy made you overpay. This character's Stone Blow carries 3 more damage per Stone, up to 9.
This worker takes 1 Stone for every card you paid a Burdened surcharge on since it last looked.
How far the capstone has been installed. At 3 it is set — and the stone falls as hard as the burial you are already carrying makes it.
A requirement met while the monument was built. Each one recorded strikes a Broken Oath off the foundation.
A requirement missed while the monument was built. The foundation swings 4 harder for each of them, up to 12.
This stone records compliance: the first measure it sees resolve each round is written down as a Kept Oath or a Broken Oath.
The next entry this scribe makes in the register lands with 1 more stack.
Each round this scribe grinds fresh pigment: its first Inscribed of the round lands with 1 more stack.
A grievance that has stayed legally active because it was never allowed to lapse. This wall's accusations carry 2 more damage each, up to 8.
Nothing on you is allowed to lapse: every affliction preservation holds in place gives this wall one more Complaint.
While this bearer still holds Block, the first affliction its side lands each round carries 1 more stack — and pressing the seal costs it 6 Block.
The first affliction another body lands on you each round is followed by 1 more stack of the same thing — forged, and never itself worth forging.
The first affliction another body lands on you each round makes the whole procession look correct: every enemy still standing gains 7 Block. A forged one counts too.
Nothing on you is allowed to lapse, and drying is burial: once each round in which preservation held an affliction in place, you are packed 1 Entombed deeper.
This embalmer wraps to what is written: once each round, an Embalmed the register made larger leaves you carrying 1 Burdened.
This body is still in process. While you are Embalmed, the first Deed you play each turn catches on its hooks: 1 Entombed.
The Guardian is working the Body: it loads what you carry.
The Guardian is working the Breath: it takes the air out of your hand.
The Guardian is working the Blood: it leaves something in you.
The Guardian is working the Name: it writes you into the register.
This entrance is legally valid. A passage check you meet earns 1 Safe-Conduct (up to 2); one you miss is 1 Trespass owed to the Finder — and three Trespass are a Claim.
These goods generate their own paperwork as they get harder to carry: 1 Paperwork for every card whose Burdened surcharge you actually paid.
This ibis repeats its rites by lunar return. Whatever affliction it last managed to lay on you is remembered as the Last Rite — and the next rite it sets is the other one.
The ibis last laid weight on you. Its cycle point repeats 1 Burdened — and its next rite is burial.
The ibis last packed you deeper. Its cycle point repeats 1 Entombed — and its next rite is weight.
How far the scarab's procession has come. At 3 the next turn is Black Noon, and the count starts again.
The chisel is set: the next positive status you would gain this round is erased outright — never gained — and a doubt is cut where it would have been. One a round.
This chisel reads favour, blessing and identity as mistakes in the stone. Once each round it strikes out the first one you would gain, and cuts 1 Doubt in its place.
Blessings entered in the royal lineage, at most 3. The Wall spends them on its own defence (+4 Block each) or on royal retaliation (+3 damage each).
Every blessing is ancestral property: the first positive status you actually gain each round is entered in the lineage as that many Royal Favor. You keep your own.

This measure is exact and this scale is honest. Meet it and the balance opens — every blow you land goes 8 deeper until the feather is raised again. Miss it and the answer is the distance: 16 damage, and 5 more for every point you were out, up to 31.
Weighed true. Every blow that lands on this body goes 8 deeper.
This one has been under the scale the whole time. A measure you miss opens its jaws — so does carrying 3 Entombed — and the next bite is the one that counts.
The next bite is the Jaws of Misjudgment — and then they close again.
The Court's permanent writer. The first affliction this side lays on you each round is entered for good: 1 Embalmed, which holds the next thing that would fade.

Each of your turns this surveyor offers two exact measures it will accept. Meet the near one and it braces; meet the far one and it bleeds and loses its cover. Miss the one you chose and you are buried 1 deeper — twice, and the boundary moves.
You took the surveyor's harder figure. Meeting it costs it blood and cover.
The next Block this body gains is reduced by this much, and the slack goes with it.
This colony is armoured by its own seals: 6 Block each turn for every one still intact. Cut through its cover and into the colony itself and you may break one — once a turn.
Break it for a ration on your next turn — and the colony eats too.
Break it and the pests are in the grain — and on you.
Break it and the paperwork burns with the chaff.
Every chamber is broken. No seal armour, an extra body in every wave — and everything you land on this colony goes 15% further.
1 extra Energy at the start of your next turn.
This colony gains 12 Block when its turn comes.

Every card whose Burdened surcharge you actually pay is labour owed. At 3 the missing hands are called — twice in a fight, two on the rope at once — and while any of them lives this rope-master braces behind them for 8.
Conscripted labour. One hand works per enemy turn, taking it in turns if two are on the rope — and cutting one down takes a burden off you and 8 Block off the rope-master.
This hand worked the rope last turn; the other one takes the next.
Three slots, and you fill them. Every application the register actually enlarges is a glyph — black for a curse, gold for a blessing — and at three the name is read back to you.
The register was spent enlarging something done TO you. The living name reads 6 harder for each.
The register was spent enlarging something you did for yourself. The living name reads 4 softer for each — and the Keeper braces 8.

This overseer measures how much of you is already wrapped. Every affliction preservation holds in place tightens the wrapping — at most twice a round — and every one you let lapse loosens it. At 4 the second wrapping goes on.
How much of you the linen already holds. At 4 the overseer wraps you a second time — and lets the wrapping out again.
One pan holds the cards you played, the other the Energy you actually spent on them. Balanced: the treasury bleeds and writes you a Credit. Overpaid: a burden. Underpaid: paperwork.
A line of credit against the treasury, at most 2. Once a turn one buys away its cover or a burden of yours — and every one you do not spend makes the closing balance 4 harder.
You have already drawn against the treasury this turn.

Every other turn this sphinx sets a riddle and shows you two of its three answers. There is no right one — answering is what buys a mark, and at 3 marks the procession opens: 18 Block off the sphinx, and a fifth more from everything you land on it for a turn.
An answer this sphinx has heard. At 3 the procession opens.
Three answers heard. Everything you land on this sphinx goes 20% further.
One of three who opened the wrong tomb. When one of them falls the survivors are preserved by what they broke into — and the last one standing is a different enemy altogether.
The opened tomb is keeping this one. 4 Block at the start of its turn for each, at most 2.

One watch a turn: measure, name, labour, burial, preservation, and then the stars are read. Clear the watch's burden before your turn ends and the keeper loses 6 — it is asking whether you have LEARNED the five words, not whether you can survive them.
The first full round of watches is done. The stars are now read at the third watch too.

Three steps, fixed and visible: the measure, the burden, and the foot. Meet the measure and work the burden off by PLAYING through it, and the foot comes down at 26. Fail one and it is 34; fail both and it is 40 and a burial.
Nothing from outside makes this thing stronger. Ever.

Three names, three wards, and a command every turn. Obey and his legitimacy is stripped 18 at a time; refuse and it heals 9 while his Authority grows. Take the ward to nothing and the name stands exposed for a whole turn.
The name in its ring. While any of it stands this king takes 20% less from you — and no blow takes it off. Obeying a Royal Command strips 18.
Every command you refused. 2 more damage on each of his own blows, at most four — and gone the moment he takes another name.
The ring is empty. No Ward can form while this stands, and everything you land goes 25% further.

Statuses.NameKey: The Name of the Two Lands
Statuses.DescriptionKey: The second of his names. South and north are both his, and he says so with both hands.
The last of his names, and the one no stone was needed for.
Spend exactly 2 Energy this turn.
End your turn with exactly 1 Energy unspent.
Lead with a Deed — the first card you play this turn.
Lead with a Working — the first card you play this turn.

Statuses.NameKey: Royal Command: Purify the Royal Record
Statuses.DescriptionKey: End the turn carrying less Inscribed and Entombed together than you began it with.

A Deed tips the pan toward the Heart, a Working toward the Feather, and at the end of your turn it judges where the pan came to rest. Nought is true balance and worth a Feather; three either way is condemnation.
Your deeds have weighed the pan down. At 3 the heart is condemned.
Your workings have lifted the pan. At 3 the heart is condemned for being hollow.
A turn weighed true. At 3 the heart is declared light.
Judged and found weightless. Everything you land on this figure goes 20% further.
The second half. The first Deed or Working you play each turn moves the pan two steps instead of one — the road is a line now.
This figure's next blow lands 6 softer.
Two blueprints after your draw, and you pick the one that governs the turn. Laid true the Monument falls a step, and every second true course costs him 8 blood and 8 cover. Missed, it climbs.
The courses that stand. One more at the end of every Architect turn, and at six the Capstone descends.
The second half. Every blueprint that resolves now adds a further step of its own — a course laid true only holds the schedule, and a course missed doubles it.
He has done the one thing he came to do. It does not happen twice.
The course you accepted: spend exactly 2 Energy this turn.
The course you accepted: play exactly 2 Deeds this turn.
The course you accepted: the first two cards you play must be of different kinds.
The course you accepted, measured for this turn: spend exactly this much Energy. Met, the Monument falls a step; missed, it climbs one.
Four seals, and a ration every turn. Play exactly what she counted as sufficient and you break a seal of your choosing; play too few or too many and the seals still standing answer for it.
Intact, an under-ration feeds her: a Grain, and 7 healed a head at the end of her turn.
Intact, an over-ration is answered with Burdened.
Intact, any failed ration is written up: 2 Paperwork.
Intact, a correct ration is merely correct. Broken, every exact ration costs her 10 blood and 10 cover.
What she has counted as sufficient for the turn ahead: play exactly this many cards, rubbish and her own seals not counted.
Taken from an under-ration. She eats 7 a head at the end of her turn.
Her next blow lands 5 softer.
Two whole turns with nothing to eat and nothing to stand behind. Everything you land on her goes 25% further.
The second half. The rations run 2, 5, 2, 5; every miss is a step of Famine and every exact ration costs her 10 blood, 10 cover and a step back.
Every ration she has counted as failed. At three the Empty Storehouse answers.

He writes down the first three cards of your turn, and at the end of his own he reads them back at you. One entry a turn may be scraped for a sheet of Paperwork. Two whole tablets read and the scroll is written over.
What the scroll says you did: 1 a Deed (6 damage), 2 a Working (6 Block for him, a sheet for you), 3 anything else (Strength for him, Inscribed for you). Nothing written is 1 Doubt.
What the scroll says you did: 1 a Deed (6 damage), 2 a Working (6 Block for him, a sheet for you), 3 anything else (Strength for him, Inscribed for you). Nothing written is 1 Doubt.
What the scroll says you did: 1 a Deed (6 damage), 2 a Working (6 Block for him, a sheet for you), 3 anything else (Strength for him, Inscribed for you). Nothing written is 1 Doubt.
What the scroll says you did: 1 a Deed (6 damage), 2 a Working (6 Block for him, a sheet for you), 3 anything else (Strength for him, Inscribed for you). Nothing written is 1 Doubt.
The scroll has been scraped and written over. He records the LAST three cards of your turn instead of the first, and each tablet's final entry is inherited into the next — where you cannot scrape it.
For one whole turn nothing may be scraped. Then the record is read, and read out.
Every affliction that leaves you is kept in the next empty vessel. Fill the shelf and she gives them all back. Once a turn, 1 Energy, you may wash one jar out — and be preserved for it.
How much of the shelf is full. Four full and she unseals them; three, once three jars are enough.
The shelf is shorter and the cycle is faster: three full and she unseals them, and the unsealing takes 12 straight out of you.
34, and 3 more for every jar still standing. The jars are not emptied by it.
She will unseal them at the end of this turn. Wash one out and there is nothing to unseal.
Weighed taken off you and kept. It comes back one stack at a time when the vessels are unsealed — unless you wash the jar first.
Burdened taken off you and kept. It comes back one stack at a time when the vessels are unsealed — unless you wash the jar first.
Entombed taken off you and kept. It comes back one stack at a time when the vessels are unsealed — unless you wash the jar first.
Inscribed taken off you and kept. It comes back one stack at a time when the vessels are unsealed — unless you wash the jar first.
Paperwork taken off you and kept. It comes back one stack at a time when the vessels are unsealed — unless you wash the jar first.
Doubt taken off you and kept. It comes back one stack at a time when the vessels are unsealed — unless you wash the jar first.
Three offices stand with him. Only one acts each turn, each lends him a function while it lives, and every one still standing at 295 is absorbed for good.
A subordinate of the King's Mouth. The Vizier gains 6 Block at the start of your turn for each office still standing, and only one office acts per turn.
This office acts on the coming enemy turn. The others stand at the Vizier's shoulder and do nothing.
The seal is in force: once each round, the next affliction to reach you lands one stack larger.
Stamped. The next affliction applied to you lands one stack larger, and the seal is spent doing it.
Every measure you miss is entered against you: 1 Paperwork, and 8 Block for the Vizier while the Keeper still stands to write it down.
The Captain of the Inner Stair is standing. The Vizier's blows land for 6 more.
The Captain was swallowed rather than beaten. The Vizier's blows land for 5 more, for good.
His next action is no attack at all: every office still standing is absorbed, and what it does becomes his for the rest of the fight.
There are no offices left to kill. Everything he swallowed he keeps, and every one of his sayings has grown a blow on the end of it.
32, and 4 more for every office he swallowed. It hands you the sheets to silence one of them for exactly one action afterwards.
The Royal Seal office says nothing until the Vizier's next action is over.
The Tally office says nothing until the Vizier's next action is over.
The Inner Stair office says nothing until the Vizier's next action is over.

The Royal Seal Bearer's warrant. While this office stands, the first affliction to reach you each round lands one stack larger. Kill it and the Vizier loses it; leave it standing when the mouth opens and he keeps it for good.

The Keeper of Tallies' warrant. While this office stands, every measure you miss files a sheet and buys the Vizier Block. Kill it and the Vizier loses it; leave it standing when the mouth opens and he keeps it for good.

The Captain of the Inner Stair's warrant. While this office stands, the Vizier's blows land for 6 more. Kill it and the Vizier loses it; leave it standing when the mouth opens and he keeps it for good.
The gauge answers to your Energy: spend it all and the water rises, leave any and it falls. Hold her at the Ordered Flood and it pays you an authority to spend on the river.

The river is gone. Fatigue 1 at the start of your turn, and she is stronger for as long as it lasts. Spend all your Energy and the water rises a step at the end of your turn; leave any and it falls one.
Too little. Paperwork 1 at the start of your turn. Spend all your Energy and the water rises a step at the end of your turn; leave any and it falls one.

The reading the state was built for. Once a round she loses 12 Block and you are paid a Sluice Authority for keeping her here. Spend all your Energy and the water rises a step at the end of your turn; leave any and it falls one.
Too much. Entombed 1 at the start of your turn. Spend all your Energy and the water rises a step at the end of your turn; leave any and it falls one.

The banks are gone. The River Takes the Boundary is her next action — unless the water is brought back down before she acts. Spend all your Energy and the water rises a step at the end of your turn; leave any and it falls one.
Earned by holding her at the Ordered Flood. Spend one on your turn and the water moves a step back toward the middle after the turn's own shift — which is how a black flood is called off.
1 Strength that belongs to the dry river. It goes the moment the water returns.
Her next action is no attack: the gauge stops answering to her, you may hold one more authority, and from then on the water drifts by itself.
Every second turn of hers the water drifts one step AWAY from the ordered middle. You may hold three authorities now, and the Ordered Flood still pays them.
At the end of her next turn the water moves one step further from the middle. From the middle itself it rises.
36, and then the water moves one more step away from the middle whatever you did about it. From the middle itself it rises.
What was done to your cards between fights is honoured here.
Repeat a card type and the witness files 1 Doubt against you.
The counter opens late: 1 Energy less this round, 1 more the next.
The first thing filed against you this fight is refused.
10 Block, and 10 more the first time you are hurt.
Your number is called first: an extra Energy and two extra cards.
Once this fight, what you do not spend is carried into your next turn.
One counter is open each round: Deeds, then Workings, then Rites. Its first card costs 1 less.
While the Fine Print is in your hand, the first card you play each turn costs 1 more.
This fight is audited: afterwards you lose 4 Gold for every point of health it cost you, up to 80.
Your fee for this fight has already been claimed by someone else. It pays no Gold.
You were sent the short way round: your opposition arrived diminished, and unpaid work pays no Gold.
Prior effort is on file: win by the end of round 3 and the claim pays 125 Gold, later only 25.
A certified original is cheaper to file: the first time you play it each fight it costs 1 less.
What the archives did to your cards between fights is honoured here.
The revision is authorized, at a price: the first time you play it this fight it costs 1 more and does half again as much.
The first time you play it each fight, the initial is worth a card and 3 Block.
Two arguments filed together. Play one and the other is fetched to the top of your draw pile, or is worth 3 Block if you already hold it.
A card that knows its own name is written back the way it was: once each fight, the first mark the archive puts on it is struck off again.
It is never discarded, and the second turn you are still holding it, it costs 1 less and does a quarter more.
A loose leaf of black ink. What it touches in your hand comes out half-erased.
Every fourth card you play in a turn is read over your shoulder, and one other card in your hand comes back half-erased.
One card in your opening hand is registered to somebody else. It cannot be filed until you have filed something else, and if you never do, it is misfiled.
This one's file is still open. The first death it is dealt does not take.
What the window lends, it lends whole: a life caught at its end comes back at a third of itself.
You are a reader here, for now: the first thing the archive writes on one of your cards is struck off again at the start of your next turn.
File the amendment while it is still half-erased and the correction is made permanent afterwards.
Three filings a turn, no more. Nothing stops a fourth; the table simply notices.
An hour that belonged to somebody else: two rounds of it are yours, and the third is when it is noticed missing.
The Librarian sent you the short way: your opposition arrived diminished, this fight pays no Gold, and there is an extra procedure waiting at the end of it.
A card the rowan sheltered. The first time each fight you open a turn with it, you gain 5 Block.
A knot tied where the road changes. The first time each fight you play it straight after a card of a different price, you gain 1 Energy.
A card somebody kept warm for you. It is never put away at the end of a turn, and the second turn you are still holding it, it costs 1 less.
A card the old stones watched. Once each fight, striking where you have already struck this turn makes it worth a quarter more for the rest of the fight.
An older right than the one that burns a card. Once each fight, a card of yours that exhausted itself is back in your discard pile at the next bell.
You have aimed something at this party this turn.
Something here is owed, and there is nobody to owe it to. Make Amends settles it like any other demand; left owing at the end of your next turn it costs you 2 HP a point, and nothing else.
The road's demand is settled at the end of this turn, paid or not.
The circle is watching how many things you do: end each turn having played exactly one real card, or exactly three. Nothing stops a second or a fourth; the ring simply notices.
Within a turn, no real card may be cheaper than the one you played before it. Nothing stops you; the line simply notices.
The next demand you settle in full grants one more leave to pass than it would have.
